criteria.name: Problem 1
criteria.description:
Use the official reference below, allowing equivalent valid proofs. Award at most 2 points. Printed subpart maxima in order: 2. Partial credit is a benchmark judgment, not an official detailed marking scheme. PDF layouts and diagrams remain authoritative.

TASK AND LOCAL CONTEXT:
1. When m doctors must each operate on each of n patients, explain why at least
m + n
2

pairs of gloves are needed, given the restriction noted in the background material that
pairs of gloves cannot be separated. Recall: ⌈x⌉is the ceiling of x, the least integer
greater than or equal to x. (Hint: think about why one pair of gloves cannot suﬃce
for three people, or two pairs for ﬁve people.)
[2 pts.]
Let’s see why we need the restriction that pairs of gloves must be worn together. Let
there be t total people, doctors and patients combined. Number them A1, A2, . . . , At, without
regard to whether they are doctors or patients. Give each person a right glove (which could
be a left glove turned inside-out), and number the gloves according to the person to whom
it is given so that person Ai starts by possessing right glove Gi. Then, if person Ai needs to
operate on patient Aj, Ai can wear gloves Gi Gi+1 . . . Gj−1 on their right hand. If j < i then
after glove Gt is reached the next layer will be glove G1. That is, the sequence i, i+1, . . . , j−1
is treated modulo t.

OFFICIAL REFERENCE:
1. Each doctor or patient must touch two glove surfaces that have never previously
touched any other person. Since a pair of gloves has four surfaces (two on each glove),
each person must use “half” a pair of gloves that no one else uses. Because pairs of
gloves cannot be used apart from each other, if there is a pair of gloves for which only
one surface of each glove was used, the whole pair is considered used, so the number
of pairs must be rounded up to the next whole number. Thus ⌈m+n
2 ⌉pairs of gloves is
the lower bound.

criteria.name: Problem 2
criteria.description:
Use the official reference below, allowing equivalent valid proofs. Award at most 2 points. Printed subpart maxima in order: 2. Partial credit is a benchmark judgment, not an official detailed marking scheme. PDF layouts and diagrams remain authoritative.

TASK AND LOCAL CONTEXT:
2. What glove(s), and in what order, can person Ai wear on their left hand to operate on
Aj?
[2 pts.]
Note that with this scheme, only t gloves—⌈t/2⌉pairs of gloves—are needed, achieving
the lower bound proven in problem 1. In fact, if this scheme is employed, all the doctors could
also be patients, and vice versa, and each person could operate on any collection of other
people, any number of times, with the operations between various people occurring in any
order. This obviously makes the problem somewhat trivial, and engenders our requirement
that both gloves be worn as a pair.

OFFICIAL REFERENCE:
2. Since person Ai−1 would touch Ai with glove Gi−1 on the right hand, the outside of
glove Gi−1 is safe for Ai to touch, and thus Ai could wear glove Gi−1 on their left hand
to touch person Ai−1. Then glove Ai−2 could be placed over it if Ai needs to touch
Ai−2, and so on. So layer Ai−1 Ai−2 · · · Aj, the sequence being treated modulo t if j > i.

criteria.name: Problem 3
criteria.description:
Use the official reference below, allowing equivalent valid proofs. Award at most 3 points. Printed subpart maxima in order: 3. Partial credit is a benchmark judgment, not an official detailed marking scheme. PDF layouts and diagrams remain authoritative.

TASK AND LOCAL CONTEXT:
3. According to problem 1, at least three pairs of gloves are needed when three doctors
need to operate on two patients, each doctor operating once on each patient. Describe a
protocol that allows each doctor to operate on each patient with no one ever touching
a side of the gloves that already touched someone else, using exactly three pairs of
gloves. Make sure to notate your solution in the notation given in the background
material.
[3 pts.]
The goal of this problem set is to ﬁnd a protocol for m doctors and n patients that
requires the fewest possible number of pairs of gloves.

OFFICIAL REFERENCE:
3. There are several possibilities. One is to use the three-doctor-one-patient protocol,
using just two pairs of gloves, giving the third pair of gloves to the second patient to
protect themselves with at all times. For example:
1. D1 G1 G2 P1
2. D1 G1 G3 P2
3. D2 G2 P1
4. D2 G3 P2
5. D3 G1 G2 P1
6. D3 G1 G3 P2

criteria.name: Problem 4
criteria.description:
Use the official reference below, allowing equivalent valid proofs. Award at most 2 points. Printed subpart maxima in order: 2. Partial credit is a benchmark judgment, not an official detailed marking scheme. PDF layouts and diagrams remain authoritative.

TASK AND LOCAL CONTEXT:
4. Explain why the problem is symmetric in doctors and patients. In other words, if there
is a protocol for m doctors and n patients using only k pairs of gloves, show that there
is a protocol for n doctors and m patients using k pairs of gloves.
[2 pts.]
5

OFFICIAL REFERENCE:
4. For every doctor-patient interaction in a given protocol, simply list the entire interac-
tion backward, turning each glove inside-out (and each pair that was inside-out back to
being right-side-in). Then it would appear the patients are operating on the doctors,
and every interaction that was safe before continues to be safe. So the roles of doctors
and patients can be reversed using the same number of pairs of gloves.

criteria.name: Problem 5
criteria.description:
Use the official reference below, allowing equivalent valid proofs. Award at most 7 points. Printed subpart maxima in order: 5, 2. Partial credit is a benchmark judgment, not an official detailed marking scheme. PDF layouts and diagrams remain authoritative.

TASK AND LOCAL CONTEXT:
5. Assume that every operation takes exactly one hour, that no doctor may operate on
more than one patient at a time, and that no patient may be operated upon by more
than one doctor at a time. Operations on diﬀerent patients by diﬀerent doctors using
diﬀerent pairs of gloves can be performed at the same time.
(a) In terms of x and y, determine the makespan of each of the ﬁve steps making
up the protocol for 2x patients and 3y doctors given in the background material.
Assume that operations from diﬀerent steps may not be performed simultaneously.
(There should be ﬁve separate calculations, one for each step, in your answer to
this problem.)
[5 pts.]
(b) If, instead, there are 2x+3y pairs of gloves available, each doctor and each patient
can receive their own pair. Then any doctor can operate on any patient at any
time, as the outsides of the doctors’ gloves and the insides of the patients’ gloves
never become contaminated and no exchanges of gloves need to take place. Com-
pute the makespan for completing all operations under these conditions, assuming
as many operations take place simultaneously as possible.
[2 pts.]

OFFICIAL REFERENCE:
5.
(a) Step 1: Each doctor must operate on x patients and each patient operated upon
by each of 2y doctors. So just from one patient’s point of view, the makespan
must be at least 2y, and from a doctor’s point of view the makespan must be
at least x. The makespan will thus be at least max(x, 2y) . But this is easily
achieved. For assuming x ≥2y then just assign the doctors to the ﬁrst 2y
patients, and each hour every doctor moves on to the next higher-numbered
patient, modulo x. If x < 2y then have each patient visit one of the ﬁrst
x doctors, and each hour every patient moves to the next higher-numbered
doctor, modulo 2y.
1


Step 2: The single pair J of gloves is used in every operation in this step, and
there are xy operations to perform. So the makespan of this step is xy .
Step 3: The description here is exactly the same as in the ﬁrst step, except that
there are only x patients and y doctors, so this step takes max(x, y) hours.
Step 4: Again, J must be used in every one of the xy operations.
Step 5: Identical to step 3, so a ﬁnal max(x, y) hours.
(b) For a reason similar to that given in Step 1 above, the makespan must be at
least max(2x, 3y) hours because that is how long it will take any single doctor
(if 3y ≥2x) or patient (if 2x > 3y) to complete all operations. And for a similar
reason this lower bound is achievable by simply lining up all the patients and
doctors and each hour having each doctor move on to the next patient.

criteria.name: Problem 6
criteria.description:
Use the official reference below, allowing equivalent valid proofs. Award at most 3 points. Printed subpart maxima in order: 3. Partial credit is a benchmark judgment, not an official detailed marking scheme. PDF layouts and diagrams remain authoritative.

TASK AND LOCAL CONTEXT:
6. Recall that the protocol given in the introductory notes allows for 2x patients and
3y doctors, and uses x + 2y + 1 pairs of gloves. Create a protocol that allows for 2x
patients and 3y + 1 doctors, still using x + 2y + 1 pairs of gloves.
[3 pts.]

OFFICIAL REFERENCE:
6. During Step 1, treat the extra doctor as if belonging to group A, wearing the J gloves.
Notice that the outside of the J gloves are still safe to use after this step, and the extra
doctor has operated on all the P patients. The extra doctor now temporarily gives up
the J gloves, which are used to protect the insides of the G gloves in Step 2. The
inside of J was already contaminated, as were the (now) outsides of the I gloves, so
no extra contaminations occur at this stage. Perform Step 3 and Step 4 as in the
protocol. Note that the (now) insides of J are still safe, so let the extra doctor wear
them again (now inside out from how they were worn in Step 1) and treat the extra
doctor as if belonging to group B to operate on all the Q patients.

criteria.name: Problem 7
criteria.description:
Use the official reference below, allowing equivalent valid proofs. Award at most 1 points. Printed subpart maxima in order: 1. Partial credit is a benchmark judgment, not an official detailed marking scheme. PDF layouts and diagrams remain authoritative.

TASK AND LOCAL CONTEXT:
7. Explain how to modify your protocol from problem 6 to allow for 2x patients and 3y+2
doctors, using x + 2y + 2 pairs of gloves. That is, allow for one extra doctor by using
one extra pair of gloves.
[1 pt.]

OFFICIAL REFERENCE:
7. Simply give the new pair of gloves to the second extra doctor. This doctor will operate
on all the P patients before the protocol outlined above begins, and then ﬁnish by
operating on all the Q patients after the above protocol ﬁnishes.

criteria.name: Problem 8
criteria.description:
Use the official reference below, allowing equivalent valid proofs. Award at most 1 points. Printed subpart maxima in order: 1. Partial credit is a benchmark judgment, not an official detailed marking scheme. PDF layouts and diagrams remain authoritative.

TASK AND LOCAL CONTEXT:
8. Explain how to modify your protocol from problem 6 to allow for 2x + 1 patients and
3y + 1 doctors, using x + 2y + 2 pairs of gloves. That is, allow for one extra patient by
using one extra pair of gloves.
[1 pt.]
There is a very complex protocol that allows 2x patients and 3y doctors to use only x+2y
pairs of gloves, thus saving one pair from the protocol given in the background material. It
will be given in the solution packet but you are not being asked to ﬁnd it. It can be modiﬁed
to show that 2x + 1 patients and 3y doctors have a protocol using x + 2y + 1 pairs of gloves,
and that 2x + 1 patients and 3y + 2 doctors have a protocol using x + 2y + 2 pairs of gloves.

OFFICIAL REFERENCE:
8. Simply give the new pair of gloves to the extra patient and treat the patient as if they
were in group P. The only diﬀerence being that when the rest of the P patients give
their gloves to the Q patients in Step 3 this extra patient need not give up the pair of
gloves—they are not needed. Alternately, think of adding 1 to x wherein the protocol
uses only one extra pair of gloves to allow two more patients, and just ignoring the
second extra patient!

criteria.name: Problem 10
criteria.description:
Use the official reference below, allowing equivalent valid proofs. Award at most 1 points. Printed subpart maxima in order: 1. Partial credit is a benchmark judgment, not an official detailed marking scheme. PDF layouts and diagrams remain authoritative.

TASK AND LOCAL CONTEXT:
10. Show that there is also a protocol requiring ⌈1
2m + 2
3n⌉pairs of gloves. This could be
fewer pairs if m > n.
[1 pt.]
Having determined an upper bound for the number of pairs of gloves, we proceed to
prove this is optimal by showing that it is also the lower bound. The proof will involve the
diagrams corresponding to the protocol.

OFFICIAL REFERENCE:
10. Given the symmetry between patients and doctors as proven in problem 4, this result
follows immediately.

criteria.name: Problem 11
criteria.description:
Use the official reference below, allowing equivalent valid proofs. Award at most 3 points. Printed subpart maxima in order: 3. Partial credit is a benchmark judgment, not an official detailed marking scheme. PDF layouts and diagrams remain authoritative.

TASK AND LOCAL CONTEXT:
11. Recall the protocol given in the introductory material for 2x patients and 3y doctors
using x + 2y + 1 pairs of gloves. Draw a diagram for this protocol when there are
4 patients, 6 doctors, and 7 pairs of gloves.
[3 pts.]
6

OFFICIAL REFERENCE:
11. For four patients and six doctors, x = y = 2. In Step 1 patients P1 and P2 contaminate
the outside of gloves G1 and G1, so arrows start at these patients corresponding to these
gloves. Likewise, there are arrows emanating from the two A-doctors with H-gloves,
and B-doctors with I-gloves.
In Step 2 the I-gloves are turned inside-out and given the the C-doctors. This con-
taminates the other side of the I-gloves, so the arrow representing them terminate
at the C-doctors. The very ﬁrst operation (which could be either of the C-doctors
operating on either of the P-patients) in this step will contaminate the inside of glove
J. Since this happens with the outside of an I-glove, the inside of glove J is actually
ﬁrst contaminated by a B-doctor, say B1.
Now Step 3 has the G-gloves being turned inside-out and given to the Q-patients
who are now the ﬁrst to contaminate their other side. So the arrows representing the
G-gloves terminate at the Q-patients. After this, all contacts occur between gloves
that are already contaminated, so no arrows will start or end at this stage.
For Step 4 no new contaminations occur. At Step 5 the H-gloves become contami-
nated on their other side by the B-doctors, so those arrows will end at the B-doctors.
Finally, since one side of pair J is never contaminated, by the instructions for creating
diagrams the arrow representing J returns to the person it started from.
There are, of course, many ways to draw the diagram just described. One way is shown

criteria.name: Problem 12
criteria.description:
Use the official reference below, allowing equivalent valid proofs. Award at most 2 points. Printed subpart maxima in order: 2. Partial credit is a benchmark judgment, not an official detailed marking scheme. PDF layouts and diagrams remain authoritative.

TASK AND LOCAL CONTEXT:
12. Explain why, for any protocol allowing all doctors to operate on all patients, every
point in the corresponding diagram has at least one arrow coming out of it or at least
one arrow pointing into it.
[2 pts.]
A component of a diagram is a set of points within the diagram for which you can travel
from any point in the set to any other point in the set by traveling only along the arrows
of the diagram (you may go in either direction along an arrow—you do not have to follow
the direction the arrow is pointing). In the diagram for three doctors and one patient in the
background material, there are two components: {X, Z} and {Y, P}.

OFFICIAL REFERENCE:
12. The ﬁrst time that a doctor operates, or the ﬁrst time that a patient is operated upon,
that person must touch a side of a pair of gloves that has never been touched by another
patient or doctor, or by an already-contaminated side of a glove. If this is the ﬁrst
time that pair of gloves has been used, then the arrow representing those gloves will
originate at that person; if the other side of the gloves has previously been used then
the arrow will terminate at that person; if both sides of the gloves are being used for
3


the ﬁrst time in this operation then the arrow will either begin or end with this person,
the choice being made at random. In any event, every doctor and patient must have
at least one arrow originating or ending with them.

criteria.name: Problem 13
criteria.description:
Use the official reference below, allowing equivalent valid proofs. Award at most 3 points. Printed subpart maxima in order: 3. Partial credit is a benchmark judgment, not an official detailed marking scheme. PDF layouts and diagrams remain authoritative.

TASK AND LOCAL CONTEXT:
13. Let s →t be a component of the diagram. That is, there is a single arrow from s to t,
and no other arrows going into or coming out of either s or t. Prove that any operation
involving s but not t must occur before any operation involving t but not s.
[3 pts.]
A component such as the above, with exactly one arrow connecting s and t and no other
arrows beginning or ending at either s or t will be called a 2-component.

OFFICIAL REFERENCE:
13. Let the arrow from s to t represent pair G of gloves. Since there is no other arrow
going into or coming out of either s or t, every operation involving s or t must use
this pair of gloves. And the ﬁrst time that s uses these gloves can be no later than
the ﬁrst time that t uses these gloves because the arrow starts at s. Assume there are
people x and y (who might be the same person) so that an operation involving t and
y occurs before one involving s and x. Since every operation involving t uses G and
the contamination of the s side of G occurs at the same time or before the time that
the t side of G becomes comtaminated, the s side of G was already contaminated at
the time of the operation between t and y. That means that y had to be protected by
some glove(s) other than G. Consider the glove touching the s side of G during the
operation between t and y.
• If that glove was already contaminated, it can’t be by s because no other arrow
goes into or out of s. But then it will contaminate the s side of G with some other
contaminant, and s will not be able to use this glove in the later interaction with
x.
• If that glove was not already contaminated, it will become contaminated by s
upon touching the s side of G during the operation between y and t. That means
another arrow must either begin or end at s.
Since all possibilities fail to allow the necessary operation to take place, the ty-operation
cannot occur before the sx-operation.

criteria.name: Problem 14
criteria.description:
Use the official reference below, allowing equivalent valid proofs. Award at most 4 points. Printed subpart maxima in order: 2, 2. Partial credit is a benchmark judgment, not an official detailed marking scheme. PDF layouts and diagrams remain authoritative.

TASK AND LOCAL CONTEXT:
14. Consider a protocol in which every doctor operates on every patient.
(a) Prove that the diagram for this protocol cannot both a 2-component connecting
two doctors and a 2-component connecting two patients.
[2 pts.]
(b) Prove that the diagram for this protocol has at most two 2-components connecting
a doctor and a patient.
[2 pts.]
Notice that in a 2-components there are exactly half as many arrows (1) as points (2).
A component with just one point has to have at least one arrow by problem 12, so the ratio
of arrows to points is at least 1. In any component of two points that is not a 2-component
there must be at least one more arrow connecting the two points, and again the ratio of
arrows to points is at least 1. In a component with n points, there must be at least n −1
arrows holding them together. So the least that the ratio of arrows to points could be for a
component with 3 or more points is 2/3.

OFFICIAL REFERENCE:
14.
(a) Let D1 →D2 and P1 →P2 be 2-components connecting two doctors and two
patients respectively. From problem 13, since D1 →D2 is a 2-component, D1 must
operate on P2 before D2 can operate on anyone at all. But again by problem 13,
since P1 →P2 is a 2-component, P1 must be operated on by D2 before P2 can
be operated on by anyone. This is a contradiction, so these two 2-components
cannot exist within the same diagram.
(b) If there are three or more 2-components connecting a doctor and a patient, by
the pigeonhole principle there are at least two where the arrow “goes the same
way.” That is, there are at least two components where the arrow goes from
doctor to patient, or two where the arrow goes from patient to doctor. Without
loss of generality assume the former, and there are 2-components D1 →P1 and
D2 →P2. Then, using problem 13 and the D1 →P1 component, the operation
between D1 and P2 must occur before the operation between D2 and P1. But
from the D2 →P2 component, the operation between D2 and P1 must occur
between that between D1 and P2, again a contradiction. So there are at most two
2-components connecting a patient to a doctor (and these two must have their
arrow going in opposite directions).
4

criteria.name: Problem 15
criteria.description:
Use the official reference below, allowing equivalent valid proofs. Award at most 3 points. Printed subpart maxima in order: 3. Partial credit is a benchmark judgment, not an official detailed marking scheme. PDF layouts and diagrams remain authoritative.

15. Assume that there are n patients and m doctors with n ≥m, n ≥2 and m ≥1. Prove
that at least ⌈1
2n + 2
3m −1
3⌉pairs of gloves are needed for any protocol that allows
every doctor to operate on every patient with no contamination.
[3 pts.]

OFFICIAL REFERENCE:
15. The number of pairs of gloves needed for a protocol is the number of arrow in its
diagram. Since m and n are ﬁxed in the problem, the goal is to determine a lower
bound based on m and n for the number of arrows. Using the information in the
paragraph preceding the problem the ratio of arrows to people in a component is at
least 2/3 unless the component is a 2-component. So to minimize the number of arrows
in the diagram start by maximizing the number of people who are part of 2-components.
By problem 14(a) there cannot be a 2-component consisting of doctors and one consist-
ing of patients. So to maximize the number of 2-components, since there are at least
as many patients as doctors, put all the patients except for two into 2-components.
Those two can be put into 2-components with doctors, as in problem 14(b). So the
maximum number of people in 2-components is n+2 if n is even, and n+1 if n is odd.
The best that can be done for the remaining doctors is to form groups of three, each
of which will use two pairs of gloves.
In this way, the minimum number of arrows that can be used is 1
2(n + 2) + 2

1
2n + 1 + 2
3m −4
3 = 1

3m −1
3. If this number is not an integer because n is not
even or because m −2 is not divisible by 3 then any extra “fractions” of gloves must
be rounded up to the next whole number. This gives the desired result.
